name: Gareth Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm farm manager at Coldharbour, two hundred and twenty dairy cows, grass and maize. The owner, Mr Hollis, is 71 and wants out, so we've got a share-farming deal: I run it, I get a wage plus a cut of the milk money, and the idea is I buy into the herd over time. Last year I talked him into two robot milkers, so my day is less milking and more watching the screens and the cows that the screens flag.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All day. The milkers flag a cow with high cell counts, and I ask the assistant what's likely going on and what the vet will ask me. I use it for grass budgets and the bank paperwork too. My girlfriend Ellie teaches at the primary school and says I talk to it more than to her, which is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's a tool, like a good tractor. Use it if it pays, don't if it doesn't. I'd say that at church and at the discussion group, and people would nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan stays my plan. Buy into the herd bit by bit, take over from Mr Hollis in five or six years. AI helps at the edges but the plan is about cows and land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Keep using the assistant every day, keep the robot milkers running, and put a bit more of my bonus into the herd each year. Maybe ten cows a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What actually worries you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bank, a bit, and land prices. Young people can't buy farms round here, it's mad. I'm not scared of robots; I'm scared of a field costing more than my grandad's whole farm did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about you and Ellie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably we'd get engaged next year. Ellie's been patient. Nothing in this picture changes that.

S0.say: I'd say it's a tool like a good tractor, so use it if it pays and don't if it doesn't. I'd say that at church and at the discussion group.
S0.think: I think my plan stays my plan: buy into the herd bit by bit and take over from Mr Hollis in five or six years. AI helps at the edges, but the plan is about cows and land.
S0.do: Keeps using the AI assistant every day and keeps the robot milkers running. Puts more of his bonus into buying about ten cows a year into the herd.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of robots; I'm scared of a field costing more than my grandad's whole farm did.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth already runs robot milkers and uses AI all day, yet his real worry is land prices and ownership. He thinks in terms of capital and succession. His personal life is steady and patient, with engagement likely next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for farms that get ahead of it. If you own the kit, you win. I'd say it straight to the young farmers, don't wait for the government to help you, get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd suit me. I'm already halfway there with the milkers. What I'd want is to own more of the herd before it all gets cheaper and everyone does it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the bank for a loan to buy thirty more cows into my share now, maybe forty-five thousand. I'd add a robot feed pusher next spring, around fifteen thousand. And I'd keep testing every new tool before the neighbours do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Keen, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at Coldharbour who'd lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The relief milker, Jess, who does weekends. With the robots she's down to checks. I'd keep Jess on because the robot can't calve a heifer at three in the morning, not because I'm soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Borrowing that much at 27, how does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a sensible bet. I'd only borrow what the milk can pay back. Ellie would want to see the numbers first, she always does.

S1.say: I'd say this is good for farms that get ahead of it, because whoever owns the kit wins. I'd tell young farmers not to wait for the government to help them, just get on with it.
S1.think: I think it suits me because I'm already halfway there with the robot milkers. I'd want to own more of the herd before the technology gets cheap and everyone has it.
S1.do: Borrows about forty-five thousand to buy thirty more cows into his share and adds a robot feed pusher next spring for about fifteen thousand. Keeps testing new tools before the neighbours do.
S1.quote: I'd keep Jess on because the robot can't calve a heifer at three in the morning, not because I'm soft.
S1.fieldNote: Gareth sees steady change as a chance to build ownership and will borrow to do it. He keeps his relief milker on for practical reasons and is quick to deny it's softness. His partner Ellie acts as a check on his risk-taking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to sort the farms that are ready from the ones that aren't, fast. I'd be honest that it's brutal. But I'd still say people should look after their own and not wait for a rescue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not ready enough. I own maybe a tenth of the herd. If Mr Hollis panics and sells to a big outfit with a robot fleet, I'm a manager they don't need. Two years isn't long enough to buy in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Mr Hollis in the first month and try to agree a faster buy-in, even if I borrow more than I'd like. I'd stop all spending that isn't the farm and put my savings into the herd. And I'd offer to run robot milkers for other farms around here for a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm usually the one ahead, and I'd feel behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Hollis in that first conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask him straight, would you rather this farm went to a company or to a lad who's worked it? I think I know the answer. Mr Hollis likes me, but liking me and waiting for me are two different things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does this mean for you and Ellie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. Two years, the wedding's on hold, the ring money goes into cows. She'd understand, but she wouldn't like it.

S2.say: I'd say this will quickly sort the farms that are ready from those that aren't, and I'd admit it's brutal. I'd still say people should look after their own and not wait for a rescue.
S2.think: I think I'm not ready enough, because I own only about a tenth of the herd. If the owner panics and sells to a big outfit, I'm a manager they don't need.
S2.do: Asks the owner in the first month for a faster buy-in, even with more borrowing, and puts his savings into the herd. Offers to run robot milkers for other farms for a fee and puts engagement plans on hold.
S2.feel: Anxious and, unusually for him, behind the curve.
S2.quote: Mr Hollis likes me, but liking me and waiting for me are two different things.
S2.fieldNote: Gareth's exposure isn't the robots, which he likes, but the ownership he hasn't yet secured. The fast picture makes him gamble harder and delays his engagement. He knows the owner's goodwill has limits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair run-up, and anyone who doesn't use it only has themselves to blame. I'd say farms should be passed on to people who work them. I'd say it at church and in the farming paper's letters page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I can own maybe a third of the herd if I push. That's enough to have a seat at the table when Mr Hollis decides. It's tight, but it's doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd agree a five-year buy-in plan with Mr Hollis, in writing, this winter. I'd add robots wherever the numbers work, feeding and slurry first. And I'd start a small business setting up robot milkers on other farms, weekends at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Busy, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change things compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm gambling. Five years, I'm planning. Give me two years and I'll borrow like a fool; give me five and I'll borrow like a farmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the biggest difference to you in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Owning the cows. The robots are the easy part.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a fair run-up and anyone who wastes it only has themselves to blame. Farms should pass to the people who work them, and I'd say that at church and in the farming paper.
S3.think: I think in five years I could own about a third of the herd if I push hard. That would give me a seat at the table when the owner decides what happens to the farm.
S3.do: Agrees a written five-year buy-in plan with the owner this winter and adds robots wherever the numbers work, starting with feeding and slurry. Starts a weekend business setting up robot milkers on other farms.
S3.quote: Give me two years and I'll borrow like a fool; give me five and I'll borrow like a farmer.
S3.fieldNote: For Gareth, time is the difference between gambling and planning. Ownership, not technology, is his whole strategy. He'd put the deal in writing, which shows he knows how fragile it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so stop moaning and start buying. The farms that are owned by families who've done the work will be fine. I'd say it at Young Farmers when I give talks there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd own the farm or most of it by 37, if Mr Hollis lives to see it through, God willing. With the robots doing the work, that's a good place to be. It's the people who only sell their hours I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick to the buy-in plan, add robots every year the numbers allow, and grow the setup business. Ellie and I would get engaged next year and married the year after. Steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry about people who only sell their hours. Who do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jess, and my mate Owen who works on a big arable farm and never touches the tech. Whoever owns the cows when the robots come will be fine, and whoever just milks them won't. I'd tell Owen that, and he wouldn't listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want from government in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not much. It's about owning things, and that's down to me. I'd want the government to stay out of the way, really, and let people buy in.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift, so stop moaning and start buying. Farms owned by families who've done the work will be fine, and I'd say that when I give talks at Young Farmers.
S4.think: I think I'd own the farm or most of it by 37 if the owner lives to see the deal through. With robots doing the work, that's a good place to be, and I'd worry for people who only sell their hours.
S4.do: Sticks to the buy-in plan, adds robots every year the numbers allow and grows the setup business. Gets engaged to Ellie next year and married the year after.
S4.feel: Calm and fairly happy about it.
S4.quote: Whoever owns the cows when the robots come will be fine, and whoever just milks them won't.
S4.fieldNote: Gareth is the one who sees a long runway as straightforward opportunity, as long as he owns capital. His concern for others, like his friend Owen, comes with a shrug that they won't listen. He wants government to stay out of the way.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be caught halfway, owning a slice and managing the rest. What would help is the bank and the tax rules making it easier for young farmers to buy into a herd or a farm from someone retiring. Not handouts, just a fair chance to own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I'd do with the time if the robots did the work. I'd go to my nephew's football on a Saturday, which I've never once done. That's the bit nobody asks.

headlineQuote: I'd go to my nephew's football on a Saturday, which I've never once done.
portrait: Gareth Petrov, 27, manages Coldharbour, a 220-cow dairy, on a share-farming deal with its 71-year-old owner, Mr Hollis, and he has already brought in two robot milkers. He uses AI all day, believes in ownership, faith and family, and wants government to stay out of the way. He's calm in a flat or steady world and would borrow to buy more of the herd. The two-year picture makes him anxious because he owns only a tenth of the herd and his engagement to Ellie would go on hold, but with five or ten years he plans a written buy-in, more robots and a setup business on the side.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be caught owning only a slice of the herd while the owner might sell to a big company.
whatWouldHelp: Bank and tax rules that make it easier for young farmers to buy into a herd or farm from someone retiring, without handouts.
